name: chirp
description: Game-oriented realtime communication backend (C++23 / ASIO / Protobuf): TCP/WS edges for game clients, a dial-out service plane for game backends, private & group chat.

paragraphs: Live demo (web chat, deployed automatically from main): — scaffold login, any user ID gets in directly; a sandbox demo account for the password login path (SDK / protocol integration testing) is available: demo / Demo-58610c42c9950348d2234db2.

When a game team wants to bring "player connections" into their own game, they typically have to build out a real-time communication stack themselves: login sessions, heartbeat-driven kick, direct and group messaging, offline messages, push notifications, and perhaps an NPC conversation channel on top. None of this relates to gameplay logic, yet every game ends up rewriting it.
chirp is built to address exactly this. The design goals, in priority order:
features: Fast integration for games. Clients connect over TCP/WebSocket + Protobuf persistent connections; game servers integrate through a dedicated server plane (outbound persistent connections + service credentials), with no…

Connecting the companion app with the game. While players are outside the game, they can chat with in-game friends, and receive voice and party invitations through the app; in-game events are pushed to the app via the…

In-game NPC AI chat. Game servers can inject messages into channels or to individuals as non-user identities (SYSTEM / NPC / SERVICE), reserving a channel for NPC dialogue, system announcements, and trade status…
Social features as standalone services. Chat, party, and friends should not be wheels every game rebuilds; chirp packages them as independently deployable, opt-in services.
